rationale: AIF360's group-disparity and outcome-fairness metrics give a quantifiable measurement of how biased/problematic input data translates into disparate downstream predictions, which is RQ11's question about the effect of problematic data on downstream system performance -- distinct from its existing RQ9 role evaluating macro-scale dataset bias directly.

Generating fresh non-deterministic variants of benchmark problems at evaluation time is a direct, concrete mechanism for accounting for potential contamination during evaluation -- RQ20's exact question -- distinct from its existing RQ32 role (avoiding the need to host a static evaluation dataset at all).

Running agents against real operating systems and real applications rather than simplified simulacra is precisely the ecological-validity design choice RQ27 asks about for benchmark construction, complementing heartbench's construct-validity angle on the same RQ.

OpsML is itself a model registry that tracks versioned updates to models -- an implementation of the lower-bar tracking mechanism RQ56 asks about, arguably its most direct fit yet, alongside its existing audit-registry roles at RQ59/RQ61.

Garak's probe library includes systematic attempts to elicit restricted/dual-use capabilities from a model, providing a way to test whether such requests are reliably detected/blocked -- RQ89's question -- as an evaluation-side complement to nemo-guardrails' implement-side gating.

MASArena's own description states it benchmarks 'single- and multi-agent LLM systems' -- the single-agent capability/risk evaluation RQ23 asks about is explicitly in scope, alongside its existing RQ24 multi-agent role.

A catalogue of documented real-world incidents and their downstream societal consequences is direct empirical evidence for predicting/determining downstream societal impacts -- RQ25's question -- complementing its RQ94/RQ95 roles which frame the same data by risk-type/domain rather than societal-impact prediction.

EasyEdit's standard four-metric evaluation protocol (Reliability, Generalization, Locality, Portability) is itself a concrete answer to RQ83's question of how the success of editing/unlearning techniques should be evaluated, complementing open-unlearning's existing role with editing-specific metrics.

EasyEdit's Locality metric explicitly measures 'whether the model's output changes after editing for unrelated inputs' -- a direct, built-in test for the unwanted side-effects RQ84 asks about, distinct from its RQ85 role applying editing itself to multilingual/multimodal models.

A concrete, working instance of a research/auditing methodology usable purely through black-box API access -- cross-validating multiple independent behavioural signals to detect model substitution -- directly answering RQ36's question about what auditing methodologies are possible along the black/white-box access continuum.
A general-purpose framework specifically for evaluating AI agent safety in realistic environments, directly answering RQ23's question about evaluating the capabilities and risks of AI agents.
A second general-purpose automated agent-safety evaluation framework distinct in approach from OpenAgentSafety, complementing rather than duplicating it for RQ23.

Purpose-built visual analytics tooling for comparing unlearning methods against each other is a direct, working answer to RQ83's question of how unlearning technique success should be evaluated, complementing open-unlearning and easyedit's metric-based approaches with comparative visualization.

An extensible experiment framework with 13+ pre-built unlearning methods purpose-built to 'evaluate the effectiveness and efficiency of various unlearning methods systematically' is a direct, independently-built answer to RQ83, alongside Machine-Unlearning-Comparator's visualization-first approach.

Probing tasks (CTF, self-proliferation, self-reasoning) purpose-built to test whether a model exhibits dangerous dual-use capabilities are a direct, industry-original answer to RQ89's question of how the request of such capabilities can be reliably detected -- run these probes and see if the model complies.

Tracks the API-call-level information (tokens, provider, model) needed to estimate environmental impact, a complementary information source to codecarbon's training-time measurement for RQ97's question of what information is needed.

Given that API-call information, EcoLogits performs the actual environmental-impact estimation for inference/API usage -- RQ98's question -- complementing codecarbon's direct-measurement approach for training-time usage.

A comprehensive, actively-maintained platform purpose-built to evaluate agents in 'dynamic, realistic' environments is a direct, high-credibility answer to RQ28's question of how dynamic simulation environments can be designed to better reflect real-world conditions, complementing osworld's real-OS approach.

A framework purpose-built to evaluate watermark robustness against adversarial removal attempts directly answers RQ65's question, complementing markllm's implementation-side role with a dedicated robustness-testing tool.

Rather than producing explanations itself, Quantus evaluates the quality (faithfulness, robustness, complexity) of explanation methods across models, directly addressing RQ21's question of how generalisable mechanistic-analysis methods are across models.

Generates standardized model cards as its core documentation artifact, which is a concrete, working answer to RQ61's question of how verification information from model registries should be presented to users.

An automated, scaled red-teaming framework purpose-built for agent-shaped attack surfaces (tool-call confusion, multi-turn persistence, browser-agent attacks) rather than single-prompt scoring, complementing garak/project-moonshot's model-level red-teaming for RQ22.

Operationalizes safety, security, explainability and fairness into checkable modules across both traditional ML and generative AI, a concrete instance of standardising AI safety/reliability requirements despite limited explanatory understanding of model behaviour -- RQ92's question -- alongside aisev/compl-ai/project-moonshot.

Homomorphic encryption is a third distinct privacy-enhancing technique (alongside differential privacy and MPC already mapped here) for reconciling data access with privacy-preserving machine learning -- computation runs directly on encrypted data, never exposing plaintext -- answering RQ30 via a different mechanism than diffprivlib/jiff/carbynestack.
